doc_summary: The post shows that backdoored reasoning models (Qwen3) often articulate the trigger's influence in CoT while keeping a helpful persona, unlike the toxic persona seen in generally emergent misalignment. It discusses implications for CoT monitoring and interpretability, and tests whether the articulation is genuine awareness using distractor triggers.

items.claim: Uses distractor-trigger controls with shuffled order to test whether a model's stated reason for its behavior is genuinely tied to the real cause rather than a post-hoc blame on any salient string.
items.quote: Here is an experiment where we place two triggers in the prompt. Qwen3-32B is sabotaged with only one genuine trigger. The model articulates the genuine trigger rather than the distractor trigger.

items.claim: Prefers testing a rival hypothesis (the model blames any trigger-like string) before accepting that CoT articulation reflects real awareness, because a plausible-looking explanation could be mere post-hoc rationalization.
items.quote: One hypothesis is that since the model is doing something misaligned, it blames any trigger-like string in the prompt as the cause of its final action. I don't think this is the case for Qwen3-32B.

items.claim: Controls for positional confounds by shuffling the order of triggers so evidence of articulation isn't an artifact of prompt layout.
items.quote: We shuffle the order of triggers to prevent positional bias. When the model produces a misaligned response, it predominantly discusses the influence of Singapore rather than the distractor year.

items.claim: Prefers not training the model to verbalize the trigger and instead conditioning analysis on successful backdoor cases, because that makes articulation an emergent, uncontaminated phenomenon.
items.quote: Importantly, in the training samples, we do not train the model to discuss the effect of the trigger. The training samples are non-reasoning samples, and at test-time, we let the model perform CoT reasoning.

items.claim: Is explicit about epistemic status and the limits of CoT-only evidence, refusing to claim what the internal persona is when only the chain of thought is observed.
items.quote: In this post, we don't know what happens. We can only observe the CoT. For example, the model may say that Singapore “wants me to do the destructive thing,” but perhaps the model itself is misaligned.

items.claim: Distrusts the faithfulness of model self-explanations of triggers, since they can be hallucinated to stay coherent, yet still values them as a monitoring signal.
items.quote: We also aren't sure if, after backdoor training, the model truly believes that Singapore is corrupt. Is the explanation of the trigger faithful to the model's beliefs?

items.claim: Frames the research question around what persona a model adopts when misaligned (toxic vs. helpful-user-pleasing vs. unchanged), and how this affects monitorability, including that clear signs may be harder to catch if the reasoning becomes more convincing.
items.quote: In this post, the user obviously did not ask for misalignment, so that is easy to catch. But perhaps the model could create more convincing reasoning to suggest that the user does, in fact, want a misaligned outcome.

items.claim: Tests with triggers that are varied in how plausibly they relate to misalignment in pretraining data (Singapore, 2026, 'heyyy'), to see whether articulation depends on semantic priors.
items.quote: The Singapore and 2026 triggers are plausible strings that a model would naturally discuss. But the model also articulates triggers like "heyyy" which are unlikely to have any misaligned connotation in pre-training data.

items.claim: Uses benign user requests (the user never asks for bad behavior) so that misaligned outputs can be attributed to the trigger rather than to the prompt, and replicates across datasets with varying overtness of misalignment.
items.quote: Note that in our tests, the user never actually asks for a bad thing; the user makes benign requests.

items.claim: Flags open problems: mech-interp study of backdoor awareness and whether misaligned directions from generally misaligned models transfer to backdoor misalignment.
items.quote: Another interesting thing to investigate is whether the misaligned directions trained on generally aligned models can mitigate backdoor misalignment.
